title: Least Hangover Alcohol, Ranked: Best and Worst Drinks by Congeners
excerpt: Which alcohol gives you the least hangover? Drinks ranked from vodka and gin to bourbon and brandy by congener content, what the bourbon vs. vodka study found, and what matters more than your drink.
metaDescription: Which alcohol gives the least hangover? Drinks ranked from vodka to bourbon and brandy by congeners, what the research shows, and what matters more.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** clear, highly distilled spirits like vodka and gin tend to cause the mildest hangovers, and dark spirits like bourbon, brandy, and dark rum tend to cause the worst, when you drink the same amount of alcohol. The difference comes from **congeners**, the flavor by-products of fermentation and aging that ride along with the alcohol. The best controlled study on this found that bourbon produced noticeably worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level. But there's a catch most "best alcohol for no hangover" lists leave out: **how much you drink matters far more than what you drink.** Six vodka shots will leave you worse off than two glasses of bourbon. Choosing a lighter drink trims the hangover at the edges. It doesn't cancel it.

**The quick ranking (lightest to heaviest hangover, same amount of alcohol):**

1. **Vodka** (especially filtered, unflavored)
2. **Gin**
3. **White rum, silver 100% agave tequila, sake**
4. **Light beer, hard seltzer, white wine**
5. **Champagne and sparkling wine** (low in congeners, but bubbles speed absorption)
6. **Red wine and dark beer**
7. **Aged tequila, Scotch, Irish whiskey**
8. **Dark and spiced rum**
9. **Bourbon and American whiskey**
10. **Brandy, cognac, and fruit brandies**

Read the rest of this guide for why the list looks like this, how solid the evidence is (some of it is strong, some of it is old and thin), and what actually moves the needle on how you feel the next morning.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on alcohol and hangovers. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. No drink is "hangover-free," and no drink is safe to consume in large amounts. If you are pregnant, take medication, have liver disease, or are concerned about how much you drink, talk to your doctor. In the US, the free and confidential SAMHSA National Helpline is available at 1-800-662-4357.

## What Makes One Drink Worse Than Another? Congeners in Plain Words

Every alcoholic drink contains ethanol, the alcohol that gets you drunk. Ethanol alone is enough to cause a hangover. It dehydrates you, disrupts your sleep, irritates your stomach, triggers inflammation, and gets broken down into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound that contributes to nausea, flushing, and that general poisoned feeling.

On top of ethanol, drinks carry other chemicals made during fermentation, distillation, and aging. These are called **congeners**. They give whiskey its caramel and smoke, rum its molasses, and brandy its fruit. They include:

- **Methanol**, a simpler alcohol that is found in small amounts in many drinks and in higher amounts in fruit-based spirits like brandy. Your body converts it into formaldehyde and formic acid, both toxic.
- **Fusel oils** (higher alcohols like isoamyl alcohol and propanol), made during fermentation and concentrated in less-refined or lightly distilled spirits.
- **Aldehydes, esters, and acids**, many of which come from the wood barrels used to age whiskey, brandy, and dark rum.
- **Tannins and other plant compounds**, mostly in red wine and barrel-aged drinks.

The general rule is simple. **The more a spirit is distilled and filtered, the fewer congeners it keeps. The longer it sits in wood, the more it picks up.** That's why the ranking above runs from clear, neutral spirits at the top to dark, barrel-aged spirits at the bottom.

For a deeper look at each congener and how it acts in the body, see our full guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

### Why methanol is a big part of the story

Methanol gets special attention because of how the body handles it. The enzyme that breaks down alcohol (alcohol dehydrogenase) prefers ethanol. While ethanol is in your system, methanol mostly waits its turn. Once ethanol levels fall, usually the next morning, the body starts processing the methanol into formaldehyde and formic acid. Some researchers have suggested this delayed breakdown helps explain why hangovers peak after your blood alcohol has already dropped to around zero.

It's also the reason the old "hair of the dog" trick seems to work for a while: a morning drink delays methanol breakdown again. It doesn't fix anything. It just postpones the hangover and adds more alcohol for your liver to deal with, so it's a habit to avoid.

To be clear, the methanol in normal commercial drinks is nowhere near the dangerous levels found in illegal or counterfeit spirits. The point is that it may add to how bad you feel the next day, not that your bourbon is poisoning you.

## The Evidence: What the Rohsenow Bourbon vs. Vodka Study Found

The most often-cited modern study on this question was run by Damaris Rohsenow and colleagues and published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010. It's worth understanding because it's the best direct test we have.

**What they did:** Healthy young adults (ages 21 to 33) drank either bourbon, vodka, or a placebo on separate nights in a controlled sleep lab. The amounts were adjusted so that everyone reached a similar peak blood alcohol level, about 0.11 g/dL, which is above the US legal driving limit. The bourbon used had far more congeners than the vodka. The next morning, researchers measured hangover severity, sleep quality, and performance on mental tasks.

**What they found:**

- **Bourbon caused worse hangovers than vodka.** People rated their hangover symptoms as more severe after bourbon, even though their blood alcohol levels had been matched.
- **Both drinks hurt sleep compared with placebo.** Alcohol of either type reduced sleep efficiency and made people feel sleepier the next day.
- **Next-day thinking and reaction-time problems were about the same for both.** The impairment came from the alcohol itself, not the congeners. Choosing vodka over bourbon did not make people sharper or safer the next day.

That last finding is the one most people miss. A "cleaner" drink may make you feel a bit less awful, but your attention and reaction time are still affected. It doesn't make it safer to drive or do anything that needs a clear head the morning after heavy drinking.

### Older research pointing the same way

The Rohsenow study wasn't the first to see this pattern. A small study published in the *Quarterly Journal of Studies on Alcohol* in 1970 (Chapman) compared bourbon and vodka and also reported more hangover symptoms after bourbon. Work by G. L. S. Pawan in the early 1970s, published in the *Proceedings of the Nutrition Society*, is the source of the commonly repeated ranking that puts brandy and red wine near the top for hangovers and gin and vodka near the bottom.

Those older studies are small and use methods that wouldn't meet today's standards, so they shouldn't be treated as precise. But they're consistent with the better-controlled 2010 work and with what we know about congener levels in different drinks. Review articles on hangover mechanisms, such as Swift and Davidson's 1998 review in *Alcohol Health & Research World*, also list congeners as one of several contributors to hangover severity alongside dehydration, sleep disruption, and acetaldehyde.

### What the research does not tell us

It's important to be honest about the limits:

- **No study has ranked all ten drink types head-to-head.** The ranking in this guide combines direct evidence (bourbon versus vodka) with known congener content of each drink type. The broad tiers are well supported. The exact order within a tier (say, white rum versus silver tequila) is a reasonable estimate, not a measured result.
- **Brands vary a lot.** A cheap, lightly distilled vodka can carry more fusel oils than a well-made gin. A 100% agave blanco tequila is very different from a cheap "mixto" tequila made with added sugars.
- **People vary a lot.** Genetics, body size, food, sleep, and hydration all change how a given night turns out. Some people get headaches from red wine at doses that don't bother others.

## The Least-Hangover Alcohol, Ranked

Here's each tier in more detail, with what pushes it up or down. All of this assumes you're comparing the **same amount of alcohol**. A standard drink in the US is 14 grams of pure alcohol: about 1.5 oz of 40% spirits, 5 oz of 12% wine, or 12 oz of 5% beer.

### 1. Vodka: the lowest-congener choice

Vodka is distilled to a very high strength and usually filtered, often through charcoal, which strips out most congeners. That's why it was the "clean" comparison drink in the bourbon study. Unflavored vodka is about as close to plain ethanol and water as you can get.

**What can make it worse:** sugary mixers, energy drinks, very cheap brands with less distillation, and the fact that vodka is easy to drink fast. Many vodka hangovers are really "too many drinks too quickly" hangovers. Our guide to [why vodka still gives you a hangover](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) covers this in detail.

### 2. Gin: nearly as clean

Gin is a neutral spirit flavored with juniper and other botanicals. The base alcohol is highly refined, and the botanicals add only small amounts of extra compounds. Gin consistently lands near vodka in hangover rankings.

**What can make it worse:** tonic water is high in sugar, and some flavored or "pink" gins add sweeteners. A gin and soda with lime is the lighter option.

### 3. White rum, silver 100% agave tequila, and sake

These are clear but less neutral than vodka. White rum is usually filtered after brief or no aging. Blanco (silver) tequila made from 100% agave is unaged and relatively clean. Sake is brewed, not distilled, but is fairly low in the heaviest congeners.

**What can make them worse:** "mixto" tequilas (only 51% agave, with the rest from other sugars) tend to carry more by-products, and tequila is often drunk as fast shots. We go deeper in [the truth about tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth).

### 4. Light beer, hard seltzer, and white wine

These are lower in congeners than red wine or dark spirits, and they're lower in alcohol per glass, which helps if you actually drink them slowly.

- **Light beer** is relatively low in congeners and is mostly water. The problem is volume: beer is easy to drink in large amounts.
- **Hard seltzer** is usually fermented sugar or a neutral base with flavoring, so it's low in congeners. Its hangover reputation comes mostly from people drinking a lot of cans quickly. See our guide to [hard seltzer hangovers](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).
- **White wine** has fewer congeners and tannins than red, though it can be high in sulfites and residual sugar depending on style.

### 5. Champagne and sparkling wine

On congener content alone, sparkling wine would sit with white wine. It drops a tier because carbonation appears to speed up how quickly alcohol is absorbed into the blood, so the same amount can hit harder and faster. Celebrations also tend to involve sugar and fast top-ups. Our [champagne hangover guide](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains why.

### 6. Red wine and dark beer

Red wine is fermented with grape skins, which adds tannins, more methanol than white wine, and other plant compounds. Red wine also contains histamine and other compounds that some people react to with headaches, often within an hour or two of drinking. Dark beers like stouts and porters have more congeners than pale lagers from roasted grains.

If red wine gives you a headache at even one glass, that's often a sensitivity rather than a classic hangover. Our guides on the [red wine headache](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) and [wine hangovers](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) go through the possible causes.

### 7. Aged tequila, Scotch, and Irish whiskey

Once a spirit spends time in a barrel, it picks up wood compounds. Reposado and añejo tequila, Scotch, and Irish whiskey sit in the middle-to-heavy range. They're usually aged in used barrels, which tend to give up fewer compounds than new ones.

### 8. Dark and spiced rum

Dark rum is made from molasses, often lightly distilled to keep flavor, and frequently aged or colored. Spiced rums often add sugar and flavorings on top. It's a heavier drink than white rum by every measure. Our [rum health analysis](/never-hungover/rum-health-analysis-complete-spirits-impact-study-2025) covers the differences between styles.

### 9. Bourbon and American whiskey

Bourbon is legally required to be aged in **new charred oak barrels**, which release more compounds into the spirit than reused barrels do. That's a big reason bourbon carries so many congeners, and it's the drink that lost to vodka in the Rohsenow study. Our guide to [whiskey hangovers](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) goes further into the different whiskey styles.

### 10. Brandy, cognac, and fruit brandies

Brandy is distilled from fermented fruit, usually grapes, and fruit contains pectin, which breaks down into methanol during fermentation. Combined with long barrel aging, that puts brandy and cognac at or near the top of congener content. It's the drink that topped the older Pawan rankings for hangover severity.

## Best Alcohol for No Hangover: Is There Such a Thing?

No. Every drink containing alcohol can cause a hangover, because ethanol itself is the main cause. Vodka at the top of our list only means "the smallest extra push from congeners." It doesn't mean none.

If you're searching for the best alcohol to avoid a hangover, the practical answer looks like this:

- **Pick a clear, well-distilled spirit** like vodka or gin.
- **Mix it with soda water, not sugary mixers.** Sugar adds calories and may make it easier to drink more without noticing.
- **Measure your pours.** Home pours of spirits are often far bigger than a standard 1.5 oz drink.
- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between each drink slows your pace and helps with fluid loss.
- **Eat a real meal before you start.** Food in the stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers what works best.
- **Set a number before you go out.** This is the single most effective step.

Two drinks of bourbon spread over an evening with dinner will almost always feel better the next morning than six vodka sodas in two hours. The drink choice is a small adjustment. The amount and pace are the big ones.

## Worst Alcohol for a Hangover: What to Avoid

If you want to keep the next morning as gentle as possible, these are the drinks to limit:

- **Brandy and cognac.** High in methanol and barrel compounds.
- **Bourbon.** High congener content, with direct study evidence of worse hangovers than vodka at the same alcohol level.
- **Dark and spiced rum.** Lightly distilled, often sweetened.
- **Red wine,** especially if you're prone to headaches.
- **Cheap, lightly distilled spirits of any color.** A bargain "mixto" tequila or harsh low-end whiskey can be worse than a better-made version of the same style.
- **Sweet, strong cocktails and shots.** Long Island iced teas, punch bowls, and rounds of shots stack several spirits and a lot of sugar, and they get finished fast.
- **Mixing alcohol with energy drinks.** Caffeine can mask how drunk you feel, which can lead to drinking more than you meant to.

What about mixing different types of drinks? The popular saying "beer before liquor" doesn't hold up. A 2019 randomized trial published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* (Köchling and colleagues) found that the order of beer and wine made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. What mattered was how much people drank and how drunk they felt. We break that study down in [the beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth). Mixing drinks mainly causes problems because it usually means drinking more.

## Dark vs. Light Liquor: Which Is Better for Hangovers?

**Light (clear) liquor is generally better for hangovers than dark liquor**, when you compare the same amount of alcohol. That's the clearest finding in this whole area, supported by both the Rohsenow study and the known chemistry of aged spirits.

The reason is mostly the barrel. Clear spirits are either unaged or filtered after short aging. Dark spirits get their color and much of their flavor from months or years in wood, which adds compounds that clear spirits don't have. Some dark spirits also have added caramel coloring, though that's not thought to be a major factor in itself.

A few caveats keep this from being a perfect rule:

- **Color isn't a direct measure of congeners.** A charcoal-filtered "white whiskey" may be lighter than a cheap vodka. Some clear brandies (like many eaux-de-vie) are still high in methanol because they're made from fruit.
- **The size of the effect is real but modest.** In the bourbon study, people still had a hangover after vodka. It was just milder.
- **Dark spirits are often sipped, clear ones often slammed.** In real life, the way people drink each type can matter more than the type itself.

So yes, switching from bourbon to vodka is a reasonable move if you want to feel a bit better tomorrow. Just don't treat it as permission to drink more.

## Things That Matter More Than Your Drink Choice

If you want to make a real difference, these are the factors with the biggest effect, roughly in order:

1. **Total amount of alcohol.** Hangover severity rises with how much you drink. This outweighs everything else on the list.
2. **Speed.** Drinking quickly drives your blood alcohol higher and makes it easier to overshoot your limit.
3. **Food.** Drinking on an empty stomach speeds absorption.
4. **Sleep.** Alcohol already disrupts sleep. A late night with a short sleep compounds it.
5. **Hydration.** Alcohol makes you urinate more. Water during the evening and before bed helps you feel better, though it doesn't prevent a hangover on its own.
6. **Your own body.** Genetics affect how fast you clear acetaldehyde. People who flush red after one drink are often slow at clearing it and may feel worse.
7. **Congeners.** Real, but last on this list for a reason.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers each of these with the evidence behind them. If headaches are your main symptom, see our guide to [alcohol headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025).

## Where DHM Fits In

If you've already chosen a lighter drink and you're pacing yourself, some people also take a supplement before or while drinking. The one we cover most on this site is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree.

Here's an honest summary of the evidence:

- **The best-known research is in animals.** A 2012 study by Shen and colleagues in the *Journal of Neuroscience* found that DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal in rats, apparently by acting on the same brain receptors (GABA-A) that alcohol affects.
- **Other lab and animal studies** suggest DHM may help the body process alcohol and its by-product acetaldehyde, and may protect liver cells.
- **Human evidence is limited.** There are few well-designed human trials on DHM for hangovers. Many people report feeling better with it, but personal reports can't separate the effect of DHM from drinking less or drinking water on the same night.

DHM doesn't remove congeners, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe. It's best seen as an optional extra on top of the basics, not a substitute for them. If you want to try it, two of the most popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with L-cysteine and electrolytes, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), which is DHM on its own. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our honest review [does DHM work?](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) goes through the research in more depth. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first. For a wider look at pre-drinking options, see [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking).

## A Simple Plan for a Lighter Next Morning

Putting it all together, here's what a lower-hangover night looks like:

- **Before:** Eat a proper meal with protein, fat, and carbohydrates. Decide how many drinks you'll have.
- **Choose:** A clear spirit (vodka or gin) with soda water and citrus, or a lighter beer or white wine. Skip the brandy, bourbon, and sweet shots.
- **During:** One standard drink per hour at most, with a glass of water between each one.
- **Before bed:** Another glass or two of water. Don't add a "nightcap."
- **The next morning:** Water or an electrolyte drink, a simple breakfast, and rest. Skip the morning drink, because it only postpones the hangover.

If you regularly wake up with hangovers, or find yourself searching for ways to drink more without consequences, that's worth paying attention to. Talking to a doctor is a reasonable step, and it doesn't commit you to anything.

## The Bottom Line

Clear, well-distilled spirits like vodka and gin carry the fewest congeners and, drink for drink, tend to cause the mildest hangovers. Barrel-aged and fruit-based spirits like bourbon, dark rum, and brandy carry the most and tend to cause the worst. The best controlled evidence, the 2010 Rohsenow study, found worse hangovers after bourbon than after vodka, but similar next-day mental impairment from both. So pick the lighter drink if you like, but remember that the amount you drink is what really decides how tomorrow goes.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What alcohol gives you the least hangover?**

Vodka, followed closely by gin. Both are highly distilled and filtered, which removes most congeners, the by-products that add to hangover severity. A 2010 study found that vodka caused milder hangovers than bourbon at the same blood alcohol level. Unflavored vodka with soda water is the lightest common option, but any amount of alcohol can still cause a hangover.

**What alcohol causes the worst hangover?**

Brandy and cognac, bourbon, and dark rum tend to cause the worst hangovers, drink for drink. They're high in congeners from fruit fermentation (which adds methanol) and barrel aging. Bourbon is aged in new charred oak barrels, which adds more compounds than reused barrels. Red wine is also a common trigger, especially for headaches.

**Is dark liquor worse than light liquor for hangovers?**

Generally, yes. Dark spirits pick up congeners during barrel aging, and the best study on the question found worse hangovers after bourbon than vodka at the same alcohol level. The difference is real but modest, and color isn't a perfect guide, since some clear fruit brandies are high in methanol. The amount you drink matters much more than the color.

**Is there an alcohol that doesn't cause a hangover?**

No. Ethanol, the alcohol in every drink, is the main cause of hangovers on its own. It dehydrates you, disrupts sleep, irritates the stomach, and is broken down into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound. Lower-congener drinks like vodka may make a hangover milder, but they don't prevent one.

**Does mixing different types of alcohol make a hangover worse?**

Not by itself. A 2019 randomized trial found that the order of drinking beer and wine made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. Mixing drinks tends to cause worse hangovers mainly because it usually goes along with drinking more, and some combinations (like brandy or bourbon) add more congeners. The total amount of alcohol is what matters most.

**Is tequila a good alcohol to avoid a hangover?**

It depends on the tequila. Blanco (silver) tequila made from 100% agave is relatively low in congeners and sits in the lighter tier. Aged tequilas (reposado and añejo) pick up more from the barrel, and cheap "mixto" tequilas made with added sugars tend to be harsher. Tequila's bad reputation often comes from drinking it as fast shots.

**Will choosing vodka over bourbon help me think clearly the next day?**

Probably not by much. In the 2010 bourbon versus vodka study, people felt worse after bourbon, but next-day attention and reaction-time problems were about the same for both drinks. The impairment came from the alcohol, not the congeners. Don't drive or do anything risky the morning after heavy drinking, whatever you drank.

**Can DHM help with hangovers from dark liquor?**

DHM has promising research, mostly in animals, suggesting it may affect how the body handles alcohol and its by-products. Human evidence is limited, and DHM doesn't remove congeners or make heavy drinking safe. If you want to try it, use it alongside the basics: drink less, choose lighter drinks, eat first, and drink water. Check with your doctor if you take medication.
